De Novo Synthesis of Oligofurans via Copper-Catalyzed
Dimerization of Ethynylethylene Carbonates
Zhengyu Han, Biao Zhu, Yuxuan Liu, Luyao Wei, Lixia Xu, Xiaolin Zhu, Jingrui Ye,* Jianwei Sun,

ABSTRACT: Disclosed here is an efficient Cu-catalyzed de novo synthesis of oligofurans, a type of valuable core unit in organic
materials. From the readily available ethynylethylene carbonates, the dimerization process allowed convenient access to differently
substituted oligofurans that could not have been easily synthesized before. In contrast to the conventional strategies, this protocol
does not rely on preinstallation of cross-coupling functionalities or presynthesis of advanced enyne precursors. Brief studies of their
photophysical properties also indicated the great potential of our protocol in tuning these properties for applications. Mechanistic
studies not only provided important insights into the reaction pathway but also allowed the identification of another protocol for the
synthesis of furan-substituted allenylic alcohols.
O
ligofurans and oligothiophenes are important core units
in organic dyes and related semiconductor molecules
(Figure 1a).
1−10
The structurally rigid electron-rich π-
conjugation system has a critical influence on the photo-
physical and electrochemical properties of the resulting
materials. Specifically, oligofuran-based organic materials not
only have superior electron transport performance but also
possess good biodegradability, making them highly attractive in
the development of environmentally friendly electronic devices
for large-scale applications.
11−13
Over the past few decades, the synthesis of oligofurans and
related structures has primarily relied on tedious procedures
involving repetitive cross-coupling from the corresponding
furyl electrophiles and nucleophiles. The less friendly stannyl
furan species were often used as nucleophilic partners, which
also posed significant concerns to the environment and human
health (Figure 1b).
1−7,14,15
The cross-coupling products were
sometimes contaminated by homocoupling products with
similar polarity, thus leading to challenges in purification.
Moreover, due to the strong nucleophilicity of the α-positions
in furan rings, the conventional synthesis of oligofurans has
been limited to α′,α′-diaryl-α,α-oligofurans II. To overcome
the above drawbacks, tremendous progress has been achieved
in developing more sustainable and efficient strategies.
16−22
Among them, Zhu and co-workers have recently reported an
elegant de novo strategy featuring the cyclization of a linear
enyne-conjugated aldehyde precursor in the presence of a
Brønsted acid or π-Lewis acid catalyst.
21,22
While such
protocols are highly atom-economic and environmentally
benign, the synthesis of those advanced linear precursors
may take a few steps (Figure 1c).
Dimerizations of terminal alkynes are important tools in
organic synthetic, particularly the “head-to-head” or “head-to-
tail” dimerizations, which serve as key strategies for synthesiz-
ing 1,3-enynes.
23−26
However, due to the propargylic leaving
group, the metal-catalyzed cleavage of the propargylic leaving
group often precedes the deprotonation at the terminal
position, thereby forcing the propargyl substitution to be the
major pathway for terminal propargylic electrophiles (Figure
1d).
27−32
As a result, the development of dimerization of
propargyl electrophiles involving cleavage of the leaving group
has remained highly challenging, thus impeding advances in
this realm.
Aiming to further simplify the assembly line, we envisioned
the possibility of intermolecular dimerization of readily

which features the formation of
both furan rings and the C−C bond between them in the same
process (Figure 1e). To the best of our knowledge, this
represents the first example of EECs simultaneously acting as
both nucleophiles and electrophiles at the same reaction site,
affording furyl dihydrofurans V via head-to-head deoxygenative
dimerization of EECs. These products can be transformed into
oligofurans VI in one pot, which holds immense promise in the
development of functional materials. Additionally, we demon-
strated a solvent-controlled dimerization approach to construct
diverse furyl allenols VII via an interrupted pathway.
With 1a as the model substrate and a Cu(I) salt as the
catalyst, we were delighted to determine that dimerization
product 2a could be directly generated (Table 1). Systematic
evaluation of different parameters indicated that, with

diisopropyletheylamine (DIPEA) as the base, and trifluor-

generated in 82% yield at room temperature (entry 1 and more
details in the Supporting Information). Other ligands, such as
bipyridine L1, phenanthroline L2, cyclohexanediamine L4, and

Interestingly, less polar solvents (THF, DCM, and toluene)
were completely unsuitable for this reaction, resulting in no

but Et
3
N led to a slightly higher yield (entries 9 and 10).
Increasing the temperature to 60 °C could further improve the
efficiency (91% yield, entry 11).
We were also curious about the possibility of the direct
formation of bis(furan) from the same pot in the presence of
an oxidant. Thus, various oxidation conditions were examined
on the crude product (see the Supporting Information for
more details). To our delight, a one-pot reaction employing
elemental sulfur in DMF efficiently furnished oligofuran 2a-F
in 57% isolated yield, thus representing a convenient de novo
strategy for the synthesis of oligofurans (entry 12).

Under the above optimized conditions, a range of EECs
were examined for this Cu-catalyzed dimerization process
(Scheme 1). Substitution at the ortho, meta, and para positions
of the side benzene rings successfully delivered the desired
products in good to high yields with excellent selectivity.
Substrates with different electronic properties were suitable,
with a limited influence on the reaction efficiency. The
structure of 2a was confirmed by X-ray crystallography
(CCDC 2303604). It is worth noting that heteroarenes, such
as thiophene and furan, could also be incorporated into the
substrates, which resulted in the formation of oligofuran/
thiophenes 2q and 2r bearing four such rings connected
consecutively. Compared with the conventional strategies that
couple each ring in a stepwise manner, our protocol is much
more convergent and efficient.
We also examined the generality of the one-pot oxidative
protocol for the direct formation of oligofurans (Scheme 2). A
series of oligofurans (2a-F−2e-F) were successfully obtained
from the corresponding EECs. It is worth noting that this is the
first synthesis of 2d-F and 2e-F, where four consecutive furan/
thiophene rings are connected at positions 2 and 3. It would
not be straightforward to access such skeletons by conventional
strategies.
18−20
Notably, these highly conjugated structures
themselves show different colors, suggesting their potential in
photophysical applications. To further demonstrate the utility
of the oligofuran products, we also studied a Diels−Alder
reaction between 2a-F and in situ-generated benzyne. This
reaction initially afforded adduct 3, but upon treatment of
TMSCl and NaI, it was further transformed into substituted
binaphthyl 4, a valuable unit in organic synthesis and materials
science.
38−41
The capability of our protocol in conveniently accessing
differently substituted oligofurans promoted us to quantita-
tively study their photophysical properties. As shown in Figure
2a, the UV−vis absorption properties of these structures were
examined. While their absorption wavelengths turned out to be
similar in the range of 250−320 nm, electron-rich 2e-F has a
notably stronger absorption compared to other oligofurans.
The emission properties of these compounds were also
investigated. A significant red-shift for 2e-F and 2c-F was
observed, but thiophene-substituted oligofuran 2d-F did not
exhibit a pronounced effect on the optical properties (Figure
2b). Photoluminescence (PL) lifetimes of these oligofurans
were also determined (Figure 2c). The PL lifetimes of 2a-F−
2e-F are 1.02, 1.09, 4.66, 1.00, and 1.77 ns, respectively. The
solubility of oligofuran 2e-F was found to be higher than those
of other oligofurans/thiophenes, indicative of better process-
ability.
18−20
These preliminary results indicated that our
products hold promise for the development of new organic
materials. The convenient synthesis from simple substrates is
expected to allow further modification and optimization of
their properties.

presence of a base, the substrate alkyne can easily generate
copper(I) acetylide species A, which undergoes decarbox-
ylation to form copper allenylidene B by eliminating CO

nucleophile to attack the carbene motif, generating conjugated
allenyl alkyne C. A similar decarboxylation may take place to
form cumulative allene D, in which copper(I) serves as a π-acid
to trigger a cyclization from one alkoxide motif together with
isomerization and protodecupration to form furan-substituted
allenylic alcohols 5. Then, the Cu(I) catalyst can further
activate the allene motif to trigger another intramolecular
cyclization to form observed dimerization product 2.
42−44
To gain more insight into the proposed mechanism, we
carried out a series of control experiments (Scheme 4). In the
absence of a base, we were able to isolate a small amount of
allenyl alkyne int-a (Scheme 4, a), presumably from direct
protonation of intermediate C. Moreover, with methanol as a
solvent, the reaction of 1a could generate 5a as the major
product (Scheme 4, b). Importantly, both int-a and 5a are
chemically competent for the generation of dimerization
product 2a under the standard conditions. int-a was cleanly
converted into observed dimerization product 2a under the
standard conditions (Scheme 4, c). Similarly, the reaction of 5a
provided 2a in 76% yield (Scheme 4, d). We were also curious
about whether the cyclization takes place prior to the linking of
two molecules, which would involve coupling with the initially
formed furan with another molecule of alkyne. Thus, 3-
phenylfuran and substrate 2b was mixed under the modified
conditions that are specific for the generation of the direct
coupling intermediate, furyl allenylic alcohol. Unfortunately,
only homodimerization product 5b was observed, but no
crossover product 5b′. This observation is consistent with the
proposed mechanism involving cyclization after intermolecular
C−C bond formation (Scheme 4, e).
In fact, furan-substituted allenylic alcohols could be useful
synthetic building blocks, but general access to furan-
substituted allenylic alcohols has previously been lacking.
45−49
The study presented above suggested that these compounds
could be generated from this dimerization reaction. Thus, we
optimized the conditions specifically for the formation of this
type of product on purpose (see the Supporting Information
for details). Indeed, with L6 as the ligand and MeOH as the
solvent, the reaction of 1a could afford allenol 5a in 71%
isolated yield (Scheme 5). The scope of this protocol was also
briefly examined. Different substituted EECs also proceeded
smoothly to form the desired furyl allenol products as the
major products.
In summary, we have developed a new de novo synthesis of
oligofurans from readily available alkyne substrates. In contrast
to the conventional strategies, no preinstallation of cross-
coupling functionalities (such as halide and stannyl groups) or
presynthesis of the advanced linear enyne precursors is needed.
The intrinsically controlled C−C bond formation and
cyclization allowed convenient access to oligofurans, a type
of valuable subunit in organic materials. The photophysical
properties of these products were studied, suggesting the
potential of this protocol in generating previously limitedly
accessible but useful conjugated molecules of this type.
Control experiments provided important insight into the
reaction mechanism, which likely involves the formation of
intermolecular C−C bonds prior to cyclization. The related
study also permitted the establishment of a protocol for the
synthesis of furan-substituted allenylic alcohols, another family
of important building blocks.

ABSTRACT: Disclosed here is an eficient Cu-catalyzed de novo synthesis of oligofurans, a type of valuable core unit in organic
materials. From the readily available ethynylethylene carbonates, the dimerization process allowed convenient access to diferently
substituted oligofurans that could not have been easily synthesized before. In contrast to the conventional strategies, this protocol
does not rely on preinstallation of cross-coupling functionalities or presynthesis of advanced enyne precursors. Brief studies of their
photophysical properties also indicated the great potential of our protocol in tuning these properties for applications. Mechanistic
studies not only provided important insights into the reaction pathway but also allowed the identification of another protocol for the
synthesis of furan-substituted allenylic alcohols.

O <sup>ligofurans</sup> <sup>and</sup> <sup>oligothiophenes</sup> <sup>are</sup> <sup>important</sup> <sup>core</sup> <sup>units</sup>
in organic dyes and related semiconductor molecules
(Figure 1a).<sup>1−10</sup> The structurally rigid electron-rich π-
conjugation system has a critical influence on the photo-
physical and electrochemical properties of the resulting
materials. Specifically, oligofuran-based organic materials not
only have superior electron transport performance but also
possess good biodegradability, making them highly attractive in
the development of environmentally friendly electronic devices
for large-scale applications.<sup>11−13</sup>

Over the past few decades, the synthesis of oligofurans and
related structures has primarily relied on tedious procedures
involving repetitive cross-coupling from the corresponding
furyl electrophiles and nucleophiles. The less friendly stannyl
furan species were often used as nucleophilic partners, which
also posed significant concerns to the environment and human
health (Figure 1b).<sup>1−7,14,15</sup> The cross-coupling products were
sometimes contaminated by homocoupling products with
similar polarity, thus leading to challenges in purification.
Moreover, due to the strong nucleophilicity of the α-positions
in furan rings, the conventional synthesis of oligofurans has
been limited to α′,α′-diaryl-α,α-oligofurans II. To overcome
the above drawbacks, tremendous progress has been achieved
in developing more sustainable and eficient strategies.<sup>16−22</sup>
Among them, Zhu and co-workers have recently reported an
elegant de novo strategy featuring the cyclization of a linear

enyne-conjugated aldehyde precursor in the presence of a
Brønsted acid or π-Lewis acid catalyst.<sup>21,22</sup> While such
protocols are highly atom-economic and environmentally
benign, the synthesis of those advanced linear precursors
may take a few steps (Figure 1c).

Dimerizations of terminal alkynes are important tools in
organic synthetic, particularly the “head-to-head” or “head-to-
tail” dimerizations, which serve as key strategies for synthesiz-
ing 1,3-enynes.<sup>23−26</sup> However, due to the propargylic leaving
group, the metal-catalyzed cleavage of the propargylic leaving
group often precedes the deprotonation at the terminal
position, thereby forcing the propargyl substitution to be the
major pathway for terminal propargylic electrophiles (Figure
1d).<sup>27−32</sup> As a result, the development of dimerization of
propargyl electrophiles involving cleavage of the leaving group
has remained highly challenging, thus impeding advances in
this realm.

Aiming to further simplify the assembly line, we envisioned
the possibility of intermolecular dimerization of readily

In summary, we have developed a new de novo synthesis of
oligofurans from readily available alkyne substrates. In contrast
to the conventional strategies, no preinstallation of cross-
coupling functionalities (such as halide and stannyl groups) or
presynthesis of the advanced linear enyne precursors is needed.
The intrinsically controlled C−C bond formation and
cyclization allowed convenient access to oligofurans, a type
of valuable subunit in organic materials. The photophysical
properties of these products were studied, suggesting the
potential of this protocol in generating previously limitedly
accessible but useful conjugated molecules of this type.
Control experiments provided important insight into the
reaction mechanism, which likely involves the formation of
intermolecular C−C bonds prior to cyclization. The related
study also permitted the establishment of a protocol for the
synthesis of furan-substituted allenylic alcohols, another family
of important building blocks.
